Co-occurrence network analyses revealed distinct interconnections between the IgG2-hi gut bacteria with 252 #virulence factors ≥1, as we discovered the existence of three different gut bacterial clusters in CD 253 patients with active disease in the NL cohort (Figure 5b). Cluster 1 consisted of several known pathogens 254 and genera implicated in CD, like Klebsiella, Campylobacter, Proteus, Veillonella and Fusobacterium 17-255 19,28 , all identified as IgG2-hi indicator genera. Cluster 2 harbored several genera normally found in the 256 oral cavity like Streptococcus, Actinomyces, Haemophilus and Prevotella 29 , none of which were 257 identified to be IgG2-hi indicator genera. Cluster 3 included genera commonly found in the intestine, and 258 among them were three IgG2-hi indicator genera, Escherichia/Shigella, Morganella and Veillonellaceae. 259

Although we found no overall significant differences in gut bacterial IgG-coating between healthy 293 individuals and CD patients, we identified a subgroup of patients with severe CD and enhanced IgG2-294 coating that harbored a distinct microbiota with several gut pathobionts as indicator genera. Amplicon 295 sequencing of the sorted IgG2-coated bacteria showed that IgG2-coating was quite promiscuous in 296 nature, and coated 84 out of the 153 genera found in CD patients with IgG2-coating of gut bacteria. It is 297 notable that we found less than 40% of IgG2-hi indicator genera to be IgG2-coated and that the IgG2-hi 298 indicator genera with increased virulence potential were identified as non-coated. IgG2-hi indicator species Campylobacter and Mannheimia associated strongly with active disease in the 300 NL cohort, which replicated in a US cohort. Campylobacter and Mannheimia were identified to co-301 cluster with bacteria in microbial cluster 1, in either the NL or the US cohort, where they co-existed with 302 genera like Veillonella that represent a top-tier IgG2-coated IgG2-hi indicator genus. Veillonella, 303 together with the other IgG2-hi indicator genera, Klebsiella, Proteus and Escherichia/Shigella have 304 previously been associated with CD 29,30,40,41 . We speculate that IgG2-coating of gut bacteria could be a 305 means for the host to delimit specific bacterial growth and invasion in individuals harboring highly 306 virulent bacteria, while the lack of IgG2-coating of certain gut pathobionts might be due to specific yet 307 16 uncovered immune evasion mechanisms existing in these non-coated bacteria. The latter may leave a 308 way for propagating pro-inflammatory responses, and thus disease flares in CD, as our findings imply. 309

A few previous studies have reported that IgG's are generated against gut bacteria by demonstrating the 313 binding of serum-derived IgG's to a panel of gut bacteria, and it has also been reported that IgG responses 314 are generated against microbes in both healthy individuals 8 and in patients suffering from autoimmune 315 disorders and CD 30 . These previous studies demonstrated a profound overlap between the gut bacterial 316 taxa that are recognized by serum-derived IgA and IgG, as we do in the present study by identification 317 of double-coated bacteria. Moreover, it was earlier demonstrated that serum-derived IgG2 can bind to 318 gut-derived bacteria, which was further supported by the presence of 35.9% of IgG2+ plasmablasts in 319 terminal ileum 31 . These previous data support our findings that IgG2 can bind to both enteropathogenic 320 and commensal bacteria in the human gut. One recent study that profiled the coating of gut bacteria with 321 IgA, IgM, and IgG, identified a significant increase in the % of IgG2-coated bacteria in CD patients 322 compared to healthy controls 32 . Although their study did not link findings to disease severity parameters 323 nor identified the nature of IgG2-coated bacteria, our combined findings point to a role of IgG2-coating 324 as a biomarker for CD patients with severe disease in which specific bacterial targeting with antibodies 325 may be a way forward to relieve disease symptoms. 326

We identified two major non-coinciding gut pathobionts (Mannheimia and Campylobacter) as IgG2-hi 327 indicator genera enriched in patients with active CD that remained non-coated despite high IgG2-coating 328 of other co-existing bacteria, like Veillonella. Mannheimia has mostly been described as an animal 329 pathogen infecting the airways, but cases of humans being infected by Mannheimia have been reported 33 . 330

Campylobacter, they are often found to infect intestinal epithelial cells as a mean to evade humoral 335 responses 34,37 . 336 The difference between bacteria that are capable of inducing IgG2 responses and become 337 and those that are able to induce IgG2 responses while avoiding Ig-coating might be a defining feature 338 in disease-driving species, since IgG2 reactions are otherwise known for their effectiveness in clearing 339 invasive pathogens, e.g. in patients with aggressive periodontitis 6 . It may be that invasive and/or toxin-340 producing bacteria, like Campylobacter, are able to initiate the breakdown of the intestinal integrity. This 341 would increase influx of luminal antigens and co-existing gut bacteria into the underlying tissue and 342 initiate a Type 1-immune reaction dominated by IL-12p70 and IFN-ɣ (due to immunostimulating ligands 343 in Campylobacter), and thus subsequently, promote IgG2-production 17,38,39 . Combined, we here demonstrated that gut bacterial IgG2-coating characterizes individuals with severe 349 CD, and is enhanced during disease flares. In this patient group we identified the distinct presence of two 350 non-coated gut pathobionts, Campylobacter or Mannheimia, that we speculate may drive the 351 inflammatory processes, and thus enhance disease severity, as they may linger in an uncontrolled manner 352 when non-coated. Specific therapeutic elimination of Campylobacter or Mannheimia may therefore be a 353 strategy to relieve disease symptoms in IgG2-hi CD individuals with severe disease burden.
